Name: Classroom Words
Description: Teachers select the sound–letter relationships already taught. Students blend and segment words, then read controlled decodable text using that sequence. Teachers listen to independent attempts, note the support needed and check transfer to unfamiliar words.
Summary: Decode new words using taught sounds
Primary outcome: Read an unfamiliar word made from taught sound–letter relationships, blending independently before using audio support.
Assessment evidence: accurate reading of new words, fewer prompts, successful blending and a brief explanation of the passage’s meaning. Game completion alone provides limited evidence.
Lesson placement: guided practice immediately after explicit phonics teaching, a short literacy rotation or targeted consolidation with a teacher.
Transfer check: Read different words on paper and spell a dictated word using the same correspondences.

Name: Think in Parts
Description: Students construct an explanation using drawing, voice, animation and interactive diagrams. Structured challenges require them to show a relationship, predict what happens when one part changes and revise after feedback. Teachers assess the accuracy and reasoning in the explanation.
Summary: Explain how parts affect a whole
Primary outcome: Explain a causal relationship with a consistent diagram and narration, then justify a prediction when one component changes.
Assessment evidence: conceptual accuracy, connected reasoning and the ability to answer a follow-up question. Assess visual polish separately so sophisticated animation does not obscure weak understanding.
Lesson placement: an initial diagnostic task, consolidation after an investigation or an assessed explanation near the end of a unit.
Transfer check: Explain a related example without replaying the finished presentation.

Name: Town Together
Description: Students investigate a public issue, compare proposals and stakeholder evidence, and calculate costs within a defined budget. In a simulated council or parliamentary process, they justify a recommendation, acknowledge a trade-off and respond to an objection. Each scenario identifies the decision-making body and its responsibilities.
Summary: Make and defend an informed civic decision
Primary outcome: Recommend a feasible proposal using evidence from competing perspectives, accurate budget reasoning and an explicit trade-off.
Assessment evidence: a recommendation supported by evidence, accurate budget reasoning and an individual explanation of the trade-off. Winning the vote is not evidence of stronger reasoning.
Lesson placement: the application stage of a civics unit, after teaching the relevant decision-making body.
Transfer check: Write an individual recommendation for a different community issue and identify the responsible institution.

Name: Wild Notebook
Description: Students investigate biodiversity, weather, water and habitats through school-ground fieldwork. They record observations using agreed methods, compare data and distinguish what they observed from what they infer. Classroom discussion tests explanations against the evidence and identifies uncertainty or further observations needed.
Primary outcome: Make a comparison supported by systematically collected observations and state a limitation of the evidence.
Assessment evidence: records another group can interpret, comparisons using actual data and conclusions limited to those observations. “We found more organisms in these garden samples” is more defensible than “Gardens always have more biodiversity.”
Lesson placement: fieldwork preparation, outdoor data collection and subsequent discussion, or a repeated investigation across a term.
Transfer check: Repeat sampling at another location or time using the same method and reconsider the explanation.

Name: TinkerTest
Description: Students identify a testable question, choose an independent variable, hold relevant conditions constant and make a prediction. They run a virtual investigation, interpret results and revise a conclusion using numerical evidence. Teachers help students distinguish simulation results from claims requiring physical investigation.
Summary: Design a test and reason from its results
Primary outcome: Identify what changes, what is measured and what stays constant; use results to support or revise a prediction.
Assessment evidence: an appropriate plan, correctly interpreted results and an evidence-based conclusion. A prediction that turns out to be wrong can still demonstrate productive reasoning.
Lesson placement: investigation rehearsal before practical work, exploration when equipment is unavailable or extension after practical work.
Transfer check: Design a physical investigation of a related question and identify limitations of the virtual model.

Name: Number Kitchen
Description: Students solve cooking challenges involving quantities, equal sharing, fractions, measurement and money. Teachers choose one mathematical focus and level of difficulty. Students predict an amount, represent their strategy and check the result, with optional hands-on measuring and sharing to test transfer.
Primary outcome: Find an unknown quantity in a recipe or measuring task, represent a valid strategy and check that the result meets the target.
Assessment evidence: correct quantities across all ingredients and an explanation of the relationship. Correct answers reached by repeated guessing need a follow-up check.
Lesson placement: guided application after explicit teaching, a mathematics rotation or a bridge between physical materials and symbolic work.
Transfer check: Solve a similar problem with real measuring equipment or counters, without the app scaffold.

Name: StoryChirps
Description: Students arrange picture sequences and record a story for a listener. Teacher prompts focus on sequencing, description or audience clarity. Students listen back, identify one point to improve and record a revised retelling. Different interpretations are welcome, with recordings retained in a private classroom collection.
Summary: Tell, listen and improve a clear story
Primary outcome: Tell a connected oral story, identify a point a listener may not understand and improve that point in a second recording.
Assessment evidence: clearer order, precise references and a revision that helps the listener understand. Preserve early and later recordings for comparison against an explicit language focus.
Lesson placement: oral-language groups, preparation for writing, responses to shared texts or short formative assessments.
Transfer check: Retell a new picture sequence to a partner and check what the listener understood.

Name: Plot a Place
Description: Students make maps of familiar and imaginary places using symbols, a key, directions and age-appropriate scale. They write navigation challenges, test a partner’s route and revise unclear instructions or map features. They also explain how the location of a feature serves a particular need.
Primary outcome: Create or interpret a consistent map, give a route another person can follow and justify one placement decision.
Assessment evidence: another student can interpret the map and reach the destination. The mapmaker can explain why a feature belongs in its location.
Lesson placement: after a local walk, within a mapping sequence or as a design-and-justify task.
Transfer check: Use a paper map during a school walk, then revise it after testing the route.

Name: Clue Canopy
Description: Students investigate illustrated stories by selecting relevant textual clues and explaining what those clues suggest. They distinguish observation from inference, consider another plausible explanation and revise a prediction when new evidence appears. Speech, drawing and writing reveal reasoning without requiring a single predetermined interpretation.
Primary outcome: State a plausible inference, select a relevant text detail and explain the connection while acknowledging uncertainty.
Assessment evidence: a plausible claim, relevant evidence and an explicit connection. Guessing the ending is less informative than explaining the reasoning.
Lesson placement: guided reading, comprehension mini-lessons, paired discussion or diagnostic reasoning checks.
Transfer check: Make and defend an inference from a fresh short passage without suggested answers.

Name: SwitchSide Stories
Description: Through teacher-guided illustrated scenarios, students explore disagreements, joining games and working together. They identify different needs, consider possible perspectives and compare likely consequences of more than one response. Students rehearse a constructive response and reflect, with room for several reasonable answers and adult support.
Primary outcome: Identify two possible perspectives, compare the likely effects of two responses and explain a constructive choice.
Assessment evidence: acknowledging multiple perspectives, suggesting a workable response and explaining its likely effect. Do not score personality, empathy or a preferred communication style.
Lesson placement: teacher-led discussion, a planned relationships lesson or preparation for cooperative work.
Transfer check: Rehearse a similar situation in a supported role-play and discuss how the response affected each person.

Name: Instruction Impossible
Description: Students write directions for a character that follows explicit steps. A test reveals missing information, ambiguous language or an incorrect sequence. Students use the visible result to revise their instructions, retest them and exchange challenges so a classmate can follow the final version.
Summary: Write precise instructions and test them
Primary outcome: Write an ordered procedure with clear actions and reference points; use a failed test to revise it so another reader can complete the task.
Assessment evidence: successful execution by a new reader, fewer missing steps and an explanation of why a revision helped. The wording matters as much as reaching the destination.
Lesson placement: procedural writing, preparation for a science method or a connection between English and algorithmic thinking.
Transfer check: Give a partner a new physical or paper-based task using only written instructions, then revise from their feedback.

Name: Edit Echidna
Description: Teachers assign one revision goal, such as clearer sequencing or stronger supporting detail. Students revise a short passage from their own writing, compare the versions and explain how a specific change helps the reader. The original meaning and the student’s authorship remain central.
Summary: Revise writing with a clear purpose
Primary outcome: Make a focused change that meets a stated writing goal, preserves intended meaning and can be explained in terms of its effect on the reader.
Assessment evidence: an improvement tied to the goal and a credible explanation of its effect. More words, longer sentences or more adjectives do not automatically indicate better writing.
Lesson placement: the revision stage of a writing workshop, immediately after feedback or in a short teacher conference.
Transfer check: Apply the same revision goal to a new piece of the student’s writing without sentence-level suggestions.
